newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Tower to list top-20 Australian fund in NZ.
newsitem.headline: Tower to list top-20 Australian fund in NZ.

text.p: Tower Trust Services on Tuesday launched a new passive fund invested in Australia's top 20 companies and said it would be listed on the New Zealand Stock Exchange by the end of February.

Managing Director Peter Fredricson said in an interview the new Tortis-Ozzy fund invested in the securities of the Australian 20 Leaders Index, giving New Zealand investors access to leading Australian companies and to the benefits offered by passive funds.

"They can invest in New Zealand dollars, they'll receive New Zealand dollar dividends, and of course it has the New Zealand Inland Revenue Department binding ruling, which says that capital gains on the sale of shares for funding redemptions or for reweighting in the index are not taxable," Fredricson told Reuters.
Initial applications for the fund would close on February 18, with units priced at one-thousandth of the Australian 20 Leaders Index on any of the five business days after that date.

Minimum initial investment was $5,000 and the fund was expected to list on the NZSE on February 28. Fredricson said there were no immediate intentions to list the fund in Australia, but that remained a possibility.

He said Tower's analysis showed that over the last 10 years, 96.75 percent of the changes in the Australian All Ordinaries Index had been reflected in the 20 Leaders Index. But the 20 Leaders' annualised gross return over the past 10 years was 13.2 percent compared with 11.9 percent for the All Ords.
The Australian top 20 index includes stocks like BHP, Coles Myer, News Corporation and Woodside Petroleum.
"So you're getting access to stocks that we really don't have in New Zealand in any sort of depth," Fredricson said.

The Tortis Ozzy fund is Tower's third passive fund. Fredricson said Tower had commissioned research which indicated that the average investor should be weighted 60 percent in passive funds and 40 percent in active funds.
He said about 50 percent of the funds under management in the United States in the mutual funds industry were in passive funds and their popularity was now growing elsewhere.
"It's certainly New Zealand catching up. I think other fund managers will get into it. We understand there are more people looking for binding (tax) rulings," he said.
Fredricson said that although the same tax benefits that passive equity funds offered would never be available in the bond market, Tower may look to launch a passive bond fund.

"I think at this stage we haven't formalised our thinking on it, but one would imagine we'd move it more into being a passive bond fund, so that it tracks a benchmark. So it may be invested wholly in government bonds," he said.
"The concept is then to give an individual investor the ability to spend $5,000 on government bonds which you couldn't really do by going out and buying them personally."
He said the initial response to the new fund had been pleasing, with a $20 million commitment from brokers.
"There's the possibility that we will get more than that on the first offer, so we're certainly hopeful of that."
Management fees are 0.6 percent maximum, fixed for two years, with a 1.65 percent application fee.
